paragraphs.heading: A city on the Euphrates
paragraphs.text: Babylon was an ancient city on the lower Euphrates river in southern Mesopotamia. Its site lies within modern Hillah, Iraq, about 85 kilometres south of Baghdad. It was the main centre of culture and politics for Babylonia, a region whose people spoke Akkadian. Other ancient sites nearby include Kish, Borsippa, Dilbat and Kutha.

paragraphs.heading: From small town to holy city
paragraphs.text: The earliest known mention of Babylon calls it a small town. It appears on a clay tablet dating to Shar-Kali-Sharri's reign (2217–2193 BC) in the Akkadian Empire. It was already a religious and cultural centre, but not an independent state or a large city. After the Akkadian Empire fell, the town came under the Gutian Dynasty and then the Third Dynasty of Ur, and early in the second millennium BC it joined a small independent city-state. In the 18th century BC the Amorite king Hammurabi founded the Old Babylonian Empire, made Babylon a major city and named himself its king. Southern Mesopotamia became known as Babylonia, and Babylon took over from Nippur as its holy city.

paragraphs.heading: Two empires and many masters
paragraphs.text: Babylon's rulers built two important empires. The Old Babylonian Empire lasted from the 19th to the 16th century BC, but it weakened under Hammurabi's son Samsu-iluna, and Babylon then spent long stretches under Assyrian, Kassite and Elamite control. The Assyrians destroyed the city and then rebuilt it, and from 626 to 539 BC it was capital of the short-lived Neo-Babylonian Empire. After that empire fell, the Achaemenid, Seleucid, Parthian, Roman, Sassanid and Muslim empires ruled it in turn, and it served as a regional capital for the Achaemenids.

paragraphs.heading: Once the biggest city on Earth
paragraphs.text: By one estimate, Babylon was the largest city in the world from about 1770 to 1670 BC, and again from about 612 to 320 BC. It was perhaps the first city to pass 200,000 people, spread over roughly 900 hectares. It stayed one of the key cities of the ancient Near East until it declined in the Hellenistic period. The last known people lived there in the 11th century AD, when it was called the “small village of Babel”.

paragraphs.heading: Wonders and doubts
paragraphs.text: Two of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World stood in Babylon: its Hanging Gardens and its Walls. The gardens supposedly existed from roughly 600 BC to AD 1, yet no surviving Babylonian writing refers to them, so some scholars doubt they were real. What we know of the city comes from digs at the site, cuneiform texts found elsewhere in Mesopotamia, the Bible, Herodotus and other classical writers, and second-hand summaries of Ctesias and Berossus. Together these give a picture that is incomplete and sometimes contradictory, even for the city at its peak in the sixth century BC.

paragraphs.heading: What the name means
paragraphs.text: The spelling Babylon is the Latin form of a Greek name, which comes from the Akkadian Bābilim, meaning “gate of the god(s)”. In cuneiform it was written with a sign for “gate”, a sign for “god”, and a final sign marking the whole as a place name. More and more, scholars treat “gate of god” as a folk etymology: a popular explanation offered for an older, non-Semitic place name whose origin is unknown. In 1955 Gelb proposed Babilla as the first name, a word whose meaning and origin are unknown.

paragraphs.heading: Babylon today
paragraphs.text: UNESCO listed Babylon as a World Heritage Site in 2019. Thousands of people visit it every year, and nearly all of them are Iraqis. But local building is spreading fast and threatens to creep onto the ruins.
